1:
The commentators begin by asking why the chapter exists, since Judah's line has already been given. Clarke treats it as a second genealogy, reintroduced with variations, and accounts for the duplication: probably different copies lay in the public registers, and the writer, finding this one held remarkable particulars, inserted it. Henry supplies a motive of another order. Ezra is most particular with Judah's register because that tribe, with Simeon, Benjamin and Levi appended, made up the kingdom of Judah, which outlived the other tribes in Canaan and had by the time of writing returned from captivity, when the generality of the others were lost in Assyria.

The opening phrase is read as tribal rather than literal. Ellicott observes that of the five named only Pharez was literally a son of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:3), the rest standing for great tribal divisions or clans and called sons in that sense. He reports the proposal to read Carmi as the more famous Chelubai, which would yield a direct line to the fifth generation, but judges the result of no special value, since it bears on nothing else in the section and Carmi is itself named among the great Judean houses. Wesley and Gill reach the same place more briefly, taking the sons for the posterity, since Pharez alone was Judah's immediate son, and noting that the names are given to show Shobal's descent from Judah.

From there the section becomes a series of identifications. Gill notes that Reaiah is the same name as Haroeh and of the same signification. Keil and Delitzsch trace Jahath as a name frequent in Levite families and make his sons Ahumai and Lahad the founders of the Zorathite families, the inhabitants of Zorah, descended from sons of Shobal (1 Chronicles 2:53). Ellicott states the relation to the earlier chapter more exactly: chapter two calls Shobal father of Kirjath-jearim and traces the Zorathites to its clans, whereas this verse connects the clans of Zorah directly with Shobal — and Ahumai and Lahad occur nowhere else. He fixes places where he can: Etam is known from the history of Samson (Judges 15:8), this Jezreel is not Ahab's capital but the town of Joshua 15:56, Gedor is the ruin now called Jedur, and Hushah is unknown though several celebrated men are styled Hushathites.

The phrase about the father of Etam is the section's textual crux. Keil and Delitzsch say the words as they stand have no meaning, and would supply the word for families from the preceding verse, giving "these are the families of Abi-Etam"; they report the Septuagint's "sons of Etam" and a further variant, and judge both conjectures. Ellicott calls the variants evasions of a difficulty and reads the phrase instead as a compressed statement that the clans named were the dominant houses of Etam.

The closing verses turn on two wives and a missing name. Keil and Delitzsch identify Ashur, father of Tekoa, as a posthumous son of Hezron, and divide his children between Naarah, who bore four sons and as many families, and Helah, who bore three met with nowhere else; Clarke finds the list defective twice over: after Ethnan he would read Coz with the Targum, since Coz's posterity follows next, and he holds that Jabez ought to be named at the end of this verse, as otherwise he stands as a consequence without an antecedent. Keil and Delitzsch agree that these verses are a fragment whose connection with the sons of Judah in chapter two is unclear. Ellicott reads the names as topography and etymology at once: Coz means thorn, Anub recalls Anab in the hill-country near Debir and seems to mean grape-town, Zobebah means she that goes softly and may be named from a brook, while Aharhel means behind the rampart and Harum the elevated, so Harum was perhaps the citadel of Aharhel's clans.
9:
A name and a verdict interrupt the register, and no two commentators settle on one man. Gill reports the Targum's addition that he was wiser in the law than his brethren, allows that the honour might lie in wealth, in strength and courage, or in his being a man of devotion, and then declines to identify him beyond one of the families of Aharhel named just before. He rejects outright the Jewish identification of Jabez with Othniel, both as improbable in itself and because Othniel is afterwards spoken of as a distinct person. Ellicott keeps to the grammar: the Hebrew verb form implies a connection with the preceding verse, so the brethren are perhaps the sons of Coz.

Clarke sets the ancient versions side by side, and they do not agree on what kind of sentence this is. The Septuagint keeps a prayer, with Jabez asking that God "give me understanding not to depress me." The Syriac turns it into something else entirely: "one of these was dear to his father and to his mother; and he called his name My Eye," followed by a blessing pronounced over him — may the Lord bless thee, enlarge thy boundary, preserve thee from evil. The Arabic runs much the same way, making the man beloved of his parents rather than a petitioner. The Chaldee differs from all of them: it names Jabez as Othniel, honourable and skilled in the law beyond his brethren, and gives his prayer a particular content — that God would bless him with children, enlarge his borders with disciples, be with him in business, and let evil concupiscence grieve him the less. Gill notices the same split from the other end, that the Syriac and Arabic read the verbs in the third person, taking the words for what his parents and friends wished for him.

On the mother's reason there is no quarrel, and two expositors draw it out. Ellicott would render the word as pain rather than sorrow, and compares the naming scenes in Genesis, particularly the mother who named her son Benoni as she died. Henry builds on that parallel. All children are borne with sorrow, since the sentence on the woman was that in sorrow she should bring forth; but some with much more than others, and usually the pain is afterwards forgotten for joy — whereas here it was so extraordinary that it was still remembered at the child's circumcision, and care was taken to keep its memory alive while he lived.

Henry gives the record two purposes, one looking back and one forward. It was a memorandum to the mother herself, to be thankful as long as she lived for having been supported through and brought out of that sorrow; it may be useful, he adds, to be reminded of our sorrows, that we may keep the thoughts we had in the day of affliction and learn to rejoice with trembling. And it was a memorandum to the son of what world he was born into, a vale of tears where he must expect few days and those full of trouble — so the sorrow in his name might put a seriousness upon his spirit, and remind him to honour the mother who bore him at such cost. Wesley reads the honour as courage and fervent piety and the record as serving both those ends at once. Henry presses further on where the honour lay: Jabez was qualified above his brethren by divine grace and dignified above them by divine providence, and they did virtuously while he excelled them all. We are not told whether it was a larger estate, office, or distinction in war, but Henry thinks learning and piety likeliest, since the families of the scribes dwelt at Jabez (1 Chronicles 2:55), a city probably named from him, and the Jews report him a famous doctor of the law.
10:
The grammar of the prayer is unsettled, and it is read as two different kinds of speech act. Gill takes the opening to mean simply that he prayed, as the Targum has it, while noting that some understand a vow — a promise of what he would do if God would do thus and thus for him. Ellicott makes the conditional form explicit: the clause is literally "if indeed thou wilt bless me," and the prayer is expressed as a condition whose consequence has been suppressed, the unspoken half being something like "then will I serve thee." He compares Jacob's vow at Bethel (Genesis 28:20) and the altar Jacob named for the God of Israel (Genesis 33:20), and reports the suggestion that the peculiar phrase about the God of Israel marks the speaker as a proselyte from the older population of the land.

Henry takes both readings in turn rather than choosing between them. Read as the margin has it, this is a solemn vow whose promise is left unexpressed, either because Jabez was afraid to promise in his own strength or because he meant to devote himself entirely; on that reading he hands God a blank paper to write what He pleases — bless me and keep me, and do what thou wilt with me. Read as the text has it, it is the language of an ardent and affectionate desire. Henry then numbers the petitions. That God would bless him indeed, which he connects with the promise to Abraham that in blessing He would bless him (Genesis 22:17), observing that we can only wish a blessing where God commands one. That God would enlarge his coast, prospering what fell to his lot by work or by war. That God's hand might be with him — and here Henry marks a contrast, since the blessing Moses spoke over Judah was that his own hands might be sufficient for him (Deuteronomy 33:7), whereas Jabez expects no sufficiency except with God's hand present. And that God would keep him from evil, the evil of sin and of trouble and of his enemies' designs, so that they should not make him a Jabez indeed, a man of sorrow.

That last petition turns on the name, and three witnesses say so. Ellicott notes that the name is explained twice over, the previous verse making it mean he paineth and this one having him pray to be spared pain, and he sets the play beside the Genesis narratives that keep returning to the meaning of Isaac's name. Wesley hears the same allusion, reading the closing verb as a plea that the evil may not oppress and overcome him, with more understood than is expressed. Gill renders the petition about the coast as a request for enlarged territory, and Wesley makes the enemy explicit: drive out these Canaanites whom thou hast commanded us to root out.

On the answer there is little dispute. Henry takes the granting to have covered his studies, his worldly business and his conflicts with the Canaanites, and makes it the ground of the verdict in the preceding verse — the sorrow with which his mother bore him was abundantly recompensed, and the son who cost her most dear was the one she was happiest in. Wesley says the same in fewer words, that God prospered him remarkably in his undertakings. Henry closes on the general point rather than the particular man: God was of old always ready to hear prayer, and His ear is not yet heavy.
11:
The register resumes with a cluster of names whose place in the tribe nobody can fix. Keil and Delitzsch say as much of the men of Rechah: nothing has been handed down about their connection with the larger families of Judah. They can at least disentangle the first name, taking Chelub as another form of Caleb or Chelubai and distinguishing him from the better-known Caleb son of Hezron and from Caleb son of Jephunneh by the added clause about Shuah — a name not met with elsewhere. Gill makes the same connection tentatively from the other direction, that if Shuah is the Hushah named earlier then Chelub was a son of Ezer, and he leaves Kenaz as either the son of Chelub or of Eshton. Clarke records the Targum's gloss on the men of Rechah, that they were the men of the great Sanhedrin, and Wesley takes them for the forebears of the inhabitants of a town not mentioned anywhere else.

On Kenaz and his line the grammarians are careful about what the word son can bear. Keil and Delitzsch argue that Kenaz was a descendant of Hezron son of Pharez, inferring it from the fact that Caleb son of Jephunneh is called a Kenezite (Joshua 14:6) and so was himself descended from Kenaz; and they hold that Othniel and Seraiah, introduced here as sons of Kenaz, are not sons in the narrow sense but more distant descendants. They find the text defective at the end of the section: of Elah's sons only one is named, and the copulative standing before that name shows clearly that another has dropped out before it. Of Iru, Elah and Naam they say nothing further is known, and they call it arbitrary to identify this Elah with the Edomite chief of the same name.

Ellicott works the same material as tribal history rather than textual criticism. Caleb son of Jephunneh is the Kenizzite who obtained a portion among the children of Judah (Joshua 15:13) because he wholly followed the Lord God of Israel; and if that Caleb and his clan were received among the Hezronite houses, then this new division of the Hezronites would afterwards be known as the house of Caleb, or simply as Caleb. He notes that Elah appears elsewhere as an Edomite princedom, as Kenaz does, and that Naam is perhaps the Naamah of the Judean town list. Gill and Clarke are both concerned to secure the man's identity: Gill denies the Targum's equation of Jephunneh with Hezron, making him another son of Kenaz and brother of Othniel, so that his son Caleb is the same who was sent as one of the spies; Clarke recalls that we have already met this eminent person and his courageous piety and inflexible integrity, and passes on the Targum's explanation of the name — that he was called son of Jephunneh because he had purged his soul from the counsel of the spies.

One clause in the middle of the list is not genealogy at all but a trade, and Henry fastens on it. Here is a whole family of craftsmen and handicraft tradesmen who applied themselves to all sorts of manufactures, in which they were ingenious and industrious above their neighbours, and the valley where they lived was called after them the valley of craftsmen — from which Henry draws the conclusion that craftsmen are not on that account to be looked on as mean men. He adds an observation about why they clustered: though two of a trade often disagree, these chose to live together, both for the improving of their arts by comparing notes and so that they might support one another's reputation. Wesley reads the title given to Joab in the same clause as meaning father of the valley's inhabitants rather than of a man.
16:
This stretch of the register is trusted least. Keil and Delitzsch introduce it as descendants of various men whose genealogical connection with the sons and grandsons of Judah is simply not given in the text as it has come down to us, and they report name after name as met with only here, seeing no strong reason even to connect Ziph with the towns of that name. Ellicott takes the opposite tack and reads the names as geography and etymology. Jehaleleel means he praiseth God; Ziph is a city of Judah towards the border of Edom, so these sons may also have been Edomite Kenizzites; and Asareel is perhaps a dialectic form of Israel, since a foreign clan might take the name of the people that adopted it.

At the next two verses the text itself gives way, and Ellicott makes the strongest case of any witness here that it is corrupt. The sentence naming the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh is, as he puts it, meaningless where it now stands, and must be restored to its original place after the opening statement about the sons of Ezra — which yields a continuous sense, with Bithiah bearing the three children whose names follow. He supports the diagnosis from the versions: the Septuagint reads the clause as "Jether bare Miriam," and the Syriac and Arabic omit the two verses altogether — which he takes to confirm that the text is faulty. Keil and Delitzsch notice the same symptoms more mildly, remarking on the peculiar singular form where sons are enumerated, and noting that two of the four names recur elsewhere but in other families.

The Jewish wife and the Egyptian wife are what the dispute turns on. Gill reads the name as meaning a Jewess, rendered so in order to distinguish her from the Egyptian wife named at the end of the verse, and reports Kimchi's view that she was the wife of Mered rather than of Ezra. Ellicott agrees that a contrast with a non-Jewish wife's sons is plainly intended, which is why the displaced sentence matters. Henry accepts the Egyptian marriage at face value and finds it unsurprising: Pharaoh was the common name of the kings of Egypt, and if an Israelite living there before the bondage began, while Joseph's merits were still fresh, was advanced to be the king's son-in-law, there is nothing strange in it — few Israelites, he adds, could refuse an alliance with the court as Moses did.

Clarke records a reading that dissolves the genealogy into allegory: the Targum takes this verse's names as epithets of Moses. Jehuditha educated him after drawing him from the water, and called him Jered because he caused the manna to descend upon Israel, and Prince Gedor because he restored the desolations of Israel, and Heber because he joined Israel to their heavenly Father, and Prince Socho because he overshadowed Israel with his righteousness, and Jekuthiel because in his time the Israelites waited on the God of heaven forty years in the desert, and Prince Zanoah because on his account God passed by the sins of Israel.

The closing verses are read as more of the same, with one argument about what holds them together. Ellicott reports that the Hebrew says the sons of Hodiah's wife, and that three added letters would give instead his Jewish wife, the sister of Naham; Naham and the Garmites and Maachathites are unknown, and Keilah is the Shephelah town famous as the scene of David's prowess and peril (1 Samuel 23:1). Of Shimon and Ishi and their sons nothing is said anywhere else. Ellicott draws the section's one structural conclusion: Ishi is elsewhere a Jerahmeelite name, but since the house of Caleb has been the principal subject throughout, and the last verse is appended without any remark to the contrary, it probably refers to Calebite clans and towns too.
21:
The register turns to Judah's third son, and the witnesses explain the order in which the chapter has moved. Gill notes that the lines of Pharez and Zerah came first, the former at length, because the honour of David and his kingdom sprang from it, and the King Messiah after it; now the writer returns to the posterity by Shelah, the only one of the three sons who left children. Wesley states the same transition in a line. Keil and Delitzsch add a grammatical note on how the chapter is bound together: the families enumerated above are linked by a conjunction and so grouped under the sons and grandsons named at the opening, whereas the conjunction is omitted before the sons of Shelah.

What follows is a genealogy of trades, and Henry treats that as the point. Laadah is named as father of the house of those that wrought fine linen, and Henry reads the clause as inserted for their honour: they were the best weavers in the kingdom and brought up their children to the same business, not aiming to make them gentlemen. He sets the formula beside two older ones, Jubal the father of musicians and Jabal of shepherds before the flood. Their posterity inhabited Mareshah, whose staple commodity was linen-cloth. Clarke reports the Targum to the same effect, that these worked in fine flax to make garments for kings and priests.

Then the record reaches back to a lost dominion, and the two expositors who take it up both read it as a fall. Wesley explains that the men who had rule in Moab held it for the kings of Judah, to whom Moab was subject from David's time, and takes the phrase about ancient things to mean those blessed days are long past: the ancestors had dominion over the heathen, while their degenerate posterity are slaves in Chaldea, employed as potters or gardeners. Henry fills in the likeliest history: in David's time, when Moab was conquered, they transplanted themselves there and held places of power for several generations, though by the time of writing this was time out of mind. Clarke sets beside this the Targum's wholly different reading, which finds here prophets and scribes sprung from the seed of Joshua, identifies Joash with Mahlon and Saraph with Chilion, who took wives of the daughters of Moab, and brings in Boaz as chief of the wise men of Bethlehem.

The last verse is a crux of translation with a moral attached. Ellicott would render the phrase about plants and hedges as the inhabitants of Netaim and Gederah, Netaim meaning plantations and Gederah being a Shephelah town; he recalls Solomon's pleasure-gardens near Bethlehem and Uzziah's farms and vineyards (2 Chronicles 26:10). The closing clause he renders literally as with the king in his work they dwelt there, which seems to him to make the potteries of these two places a royal establishment, as those of Sèvres used to be. Keil and Delitzsch leave open whether the demonstrative covers all Shelah's descendants or only those just named, reporting Bertheau's preference for the narrower reference. Gill reads the verse as a decline, the posterity of men once famous in their day now in mean employments. Clarke, having quoted the Targum's reading that these were the disciples of the law, says plainly that he is afraid the paraphrase gives as little light as the text itself. Henry presses the moral hardest: they dwelt with the king for his work, got a good livelihood by their industry, and therefore cared not to return with their brethren when the captivity expired — and those were unworthy the name of Israelites who would dwell among plants and hedges rather than take the pains of returning to Canaan. Those who now have dominion, he adds, do not know what their posterity may be reduced to.
24:
Simeon is taken up next, and Gill explains the order: his account comes before Reuben's because his inheritance lay within the tribe of Judah. The list itself does not match the Pentateuch, and that is handled three different ways. Ellicott sets out the three earlier lists — Genesis and Exodus name six sons, while Numbers agrees with Chronicles in naming five, Ohad being dropped; where this verse has Jarib, Numbers has Jachin; and Genesis and Exodus read Jemuel and Zohar where this reads Nemuel and Zerah. Gill notices the same substitution on the first name. Keil and Delitzsch explain the shorter list rather than merely recording it: only the five who actually founded families are named, and Ohad is absent even from the Numbers census, clearly because his posterity had either died out or dwindled so far that it could form no independent family. Clarke declines the whole exercise. The genealogy is very different from the earlier ones, which may be because the same person bore several names; to reconcile them is impossible, and to attempt it useless.

One son is singled out by his mother's origin. Ellicott notes that Exodus calls Shaul the son of a Canaanitess, and draws the consequence that matters for the rest of the chapter: the mixed race of Shaul was the only Simeonite clan that became populous, and the other clans are not noticed further by this genealogy. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same man from the other side, taking the next name without doubt for the son of that same Shaul whom Genesis and Exodus distinguish by his mother, and tracing his family down through six generations. They note that the list is broken into two groups by the clause about the sons of Mishma, and admit that the reason for the division is unknown. Gill walks the same chain of descent plainly, son by son.

The chapter then says something about Simeon that is not genealogy but history, and every witness stops on it. Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters — none of them named, as Gill observes — and by them became the father of a numerous race; but his brethren, meaning the other Simeonite clans, had not many children, so that the tribe as a whole never multiplied as Judah did. Ellicott would render the clause as that they did not multiply their whole clan, taking the word for clan here in the wider sense of tribe, and he confirms the remark from what is otherwise known: Simeon was never historically important and appears in the end to have been absorbed into Judah, within whose territory its domain lay.

Clarke supplies the figures, and they are blunt. At the first census the families of Simeon numbered fifty-nine thousand three hundred against Judah's seventy-four thousand six hundred; at the second, Judah had risen to seventy-six thousand five hundred, an increase of nineteen hundred, while Simeon had fallen to twenty-two thousand two hundred, a decrease of thirty-seven thousand one hundred — at that point the smallest tribe in Israel. Two witnesses refer the decline to a word spoken long before. Ellicott sets Jacob's sentence beside it, that he would divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel (Genesis 49:7); Wesley ascribes the failure to increase directly to that curse, and adds a second sign of the same disfavour, that Moses passed Simeon over when he blessed all the other tribes. Henry takes the comparison in the opposite direction and makes it a lesson for the reader rather than a verdict on the tribe: it is said of Simeon that they increased greatly, though not like the children of Judah, and those whom God increases ought to be thankful even when they see others more increased than themselves.
28:
The list of Simeon's towns is the same list Joshua gives, and the commentators spend their attention on the places where the two do not quite match. Keil and Delitzsch set out the structure: these were the ancient dwelling-places received within Judah's domain at the division of the land (Joshua 19:1), eighteen cities in two groups of thirteen and five, in the same order in both books — the one difference being that Joshua reckons four in the second group though his first contains fourteen names. Ellicott accounts for the discrepancy: Joshua adds Sheba after Beer-sheba, an obviously mistaken repetition which makes fourteen where the summary says thirteen.

Ellicott then works through the names as topography and etymology, and the result reads like a gazetteer. Beer-sheba and Moladah he can place, the latter south of Hebron, while Hazar-shual, the fox-village, is unknown. Hormah is the ancient Zephath, and Ziklag lies east of it. Beth-marcaboth is the house of chariots and Hazar-susim the village of horses. Beth-birei he takes for a corrupt writing of Beth-lebaoth, the house of lionesses, contracted elsewhere to Lebaoth — and he observes that there were in fact lions in the wilds of Judah (1 Samuel 17:34). Shaaraim, the two gates, he identifies with Sharuhen, a name known from the Egyptian inscriptions. Keil and Delitzsch are more cautious about the closing group, holding that the position of those places has not yet been certainly ascertained.

Why five cities stand apart from the thirteen is a question the witnesses answer from the Jewish expositors. Ellicott reports that Rashi and Kimchi assert the thirteen were lost to the Simeonites from the time of David while these five remained in their possession, and notes that the separation is made in Joshua as well as here. Gill follows Kimchi and draws the consequence: these were all that remained for them, so they had to seek new settlements for themselves and their flocks. Both grammarians note that Joshua counts four here rather than five, with one name differing and another absent, and Ellicott suggests that Etam may be a mistake for Ether.

The note that these were their cities only until David's reign draws three different explanations, and they are not compatible. Clarke holds that David took some of the Simeonite cities and added them to Judah, and that because the tribe had withdrawn its allegiance, the kings of Judah pushed their domination into its territory as far as they could — which is why the Simeonites had to seek pasture at Gedor and in the mountains of Seir. Wesley blames the tribe rather than the crown: several of these cities, though assigned to Simeon by Joshua, were through that tribe's sloth never taken from the Philistines until David's time, and David, finding the right forfeited by neglect, gave them to his own tribe — Ziklag being in Philistine hands in his day and given to him by them. Henry reads the clause as marking a voluntary departure instead: when the ten tribes revolted from the house of David, many of the Simeonites quitted these cities because they lay within Judah, and settled elsewhere.

The section ends with a word about records rather than places, and both grammarians stop on it. Ellicott renders the closing phrase as that they had their own registration, and draws out what it implies: though their settlements lay inside the territory of Judah, their clans were enrolled as belonging to a distinct tribe. Keil and Delitzsch say the same more pointedly: though only a small tribe dwelling in the midst of Judah, they yet had a family register of their own. Ellicott adds that the place named at the end is Joshua's Baalath-beer, the lady of the well, and that the same passage seems to name this group of villages Ramah of the southland.
34:
A roll of names is given without any explanation of who the men were, and the witnesses treat the list as a preface rather than an appendix. Keil and Delitzsch read it that way explicitly: the verses record the emigrations of Simeonite families into other districts, and the names belong to an expedition of conquest undertaken in the time of Hezekiah, which the chapter will describe in a moment. They count thirteen princes of the tribe, and note that although the families of some are traced through several generations, in no case are they traced far enough to show how they connect with the Simeonite families enumerated earlier in the chapter. That gap is characteristic of the whole chapter, and they do not try to close it.

Gill supplies what the names themselves will not. These, with those that follow to the end of the chapter, were famous men in the tribe of Simeon, of rank and dignity and eminent for courage and valour, as the latter part of the chapter testifies — though they are nowhere else taken notice of in Scripture. He adds one curiosity of philology, observing with Fabritius that the name Jamlech is not very different from Jamblichus, the name of a famous Platonic philosopher. Ellicott glosses another of the names in the same register: Jaakobah is literally "to Jacob," a patronymic formed from Jacob much as the English surname Jacobs is formed.

Henry sets the increase against the tribe's history and finds a providence in it. When those of Simeon who had revolted from the house of David were carried captive into Assyria with the rest, those who adhered to Judah were remarkably owned of God and prospered in their endeavours to enlarge their coasts; and it was in the days of Hezekiah, he observes, that a generation of Simeonites whose tribe had long crouched and truckled was animated to make these bold efforts. The chapter has just said that this tribe did not multiply like the children of Judah; the house of these particular fathers increasing greatly is therefore the one place where the register records Simeon growing rather than shrinking, and it is immediately followed by the men going out to find room.
38:
The roll closes with a summary the grammarians read as the chapter's hinge. Keil and Delitzsch render it as that these men, named one by one, were princes in their families, whose fathers' houses had increased to a multitude, and they take the clause about going out as continuous with it — so the increase is the reason for the expedition, not a separate fact. Gill takes the title plainly: the principal men among them, heads of their fathers' houses.

What follows is that expedition, and the first question is its direction. The usual rendering sends them to the entrance of Gedor; Keil and Delitzsch reject it, arguing that the word means not entrance but the west, abridged from the going in of the sun, since the matching term means the sunrise. On their reading the princes went westward from Gedor to the east side of the valley — though the locality itself, they admit, is unknown.

What they found is described in terms worth dwelling on. Ellicott renders the phrase about the land literally as broad of both hands, an open plain, and compares the quiet of Laish, which the Danites took by surprise. Those of Ham he takes for Canaanites, and the words about old time for before the Simeonite invasion. Wesley draws a practical consequence: the clause gives the reason they went and possessed the place, since it lay not in the hands of their brethren of Judah but of a people they had authority to expel. Henry turns the description into a thanksgiving: those who dwell in a country wide and quiet and peaceable have reason to own themselves indebted to the God who appoints the bounds of our habitation — Wesley's conclusion too.

Neither Henry nor Keil and Delitzsch let that quiet pass. Henry observes that they found fat pastures and yet the land was quiet: even while the kings of Assyria disturbed all their neighbours this land escaped their alarms, its people being shepherds who molested nobody and were therefore unmolested — until the Simeonites drove them out and succeeded them not only in the plenty of their land but in its peace. Keil and Delitzsch describe the Simeonite princes and their people falling upon the peaceful little people of the Hamites. Henry nevertheless reads the expedition as a mark of favour on the reign that saw it: as Hezekiah's kingdom prospered, so did particular families, and a generation of Simeonites whose tribe had long crouched and truckled was animated to these bold efforts.

One clause here is textually unsettled. Ellicott reports that the Hebrew text reads the wells where the margin reads the Maonites, two very similar words, with the Septuagint supporting the Minaeans; he judges the margin probably correct, since the verb the Syriac rendering requires is wanting in the Hebrew, identifying the Maonites as sojourners from Maon near Petra.

A second and smaller expedition closes the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch describe five hundred men marching to Mount Seir under four chiefs, smiting the Amalekite remnant and dwelling there. Gill and Clarke identify those survivors as escapees from the wars of Saul and David. Ellicott argues that the two expeditions belong together: the time of this one is not stated, but for that reason it is likely nearly contemporaneous, and the five hundred seem to have belonged to the clans that had already smitten the Hamites. Henry closes on the longest view. The curses on Ham and on Amalek found a further accomplishment here when they seemed dormant; so did the curse on Simeon, that he should be divided and scattered (Genesis 49:7) — yet to Simeon it was turned into a blessing, since the families who transplanted themselves into those distant countries are said to dwell there to this day, by which it seems they escaped the captivity's calamities. Providence sometimes sends out of trouble those designed for preservation.
